title: Which Picture of DNA Should You Trust?

scenes.tts: Several pictures can all represent D N A. Which one should you trust? The answer changes with your question. Keep one short sample in view while its pictures change.
scenes.caption: Several pictures can all represent DNA. Which one should you trust? The answer changes with your question. Keep one short sample in view while its pictures change.
scenes.narration: Several pictures can all represent DNA. Which one should you trust? The answer changes with your question. Keep one short sample in view while its pictures change.
scenes.visual: Build the carried 16:9 world and colour map used by both films. DNA base blocks are BLUE; backbones and outlines GREY; the moving question lens YELLOW; shown features GREEN; omitted features ORANGE; evidence PURPLE. Everything is labelled 'schematic'. A large mystery box labelled 'DNA sample' fills the middle. Around it, empty frames labelled 'pairing', 'shape', 'order' and 'occupied space' orbit slowly. On the question, a yellow lens sweeps across the frames while the sample box keeps gently pulsing. No molecular structure is drawn.
The title 'Which Picture of DNA Should You Trust?' appears above the carried mystery box. The yellow lens keeps moving and the labelled question frames drift slowly.

scenes.tts: A scientific model is a simplified representation. It helps explain or predict something real. It is a tool, not a perfect copy. Every tool has a job and a limit.
scenes.caption: A scientific model is a simplified representation. It helps explain or predict something real. It is a tool, not a perfect copy. Every tool has a job and a limit.
scenes.narration: A scientific model is a simplified representation. It helps explain or predict something real. It is a tool, not a perfect copy. Every tool has a job and a limit.
scenes.visual: The DNA sample box slides left but remains visible. A large toolbox grows beside it. A plain labelled card 'MODEL' rises from the box and locks into the yellow question lens. Green text 'shows' appears on one side of the card and orange text 'leaves out' on the other. The two labels rock like a balance while the toolbox handle moves gently.

scenes.tts: Ask which bases face each other. A flat ladder helps. Labelled base blocks form rungs between plain backbone bars. Pairing is clear, but the twist and atoms are gone.
scenes.caption: Ask which bases face each other. A flat ladder helps. Labelled base blocks form rungs between plain backbone bars. Pairing is clear, but the twist and atoms are gone.
scenes.narration: Ask which bases face each other. A flat ladder helps. Labelled base blocks form rungs between plain backbone bars. Pairing is clear, but the twist and atoms are gone.
scenes.visual: The yellow lens clicks onto 'pairing'. The model card expands into two tall GREY bars joined by BLUE labelled blocks: A opposite T and G opposite C. These are blocks, not atoms. Each matched rung glows GREEN. An ORANGE curtain labelled 'twist and atoms' covers a blank side panel. The DNA sample box stays at left.

scenes.tts: Ask for base order instead. The ladder folds into a straight letter strip. Comparing positions becomes easy. Shape, size, and the partner strand disappear from this view.
scenes.caption: Ask for base order instead. The ladder folds into a straight letter strip. Comparing positions becomes easy. Shape, size, and the partner strand disappear from this view.
scenes.narration: Ask for base order instead. The ladder folds into a straight letter strip. Comparing positions becomes easy. Shape, size, and the partner strand disappear from this view.
scenes.visual: The lens slides from 'pairing' to 'order'. The ladder's BLUE rungs detach, rotate and settle into one horizontal letter strip, shown alone while the partner strand stays covered. Then a separately labelled 'comparison sequence' strip slides in beneath it; matching positions glow GREEN and differences glow YELLOW. The GREY backbone bars fade behind an ORANGE panel labelled 'shape, size, partner'. The sample box keeps pulsing.

scenes.tts: A ribbon model answers a shape question by showing coiling strands. A space-filling model shows occupied space. Neither is best for reading the exact order.
scenes.caption: A ribbon model answers a shape question by showing coiling strands. A space-filling model shows occupied space. Neither is best for reading the exact order.
scenes.narration: A ribbon model answers a shape question by showing coiling strands. A space-filling model shows occupied space. Neither is best for reading the exact order.
scenes.visual: The lens visits 'shape'. A large rectangular card labelled 'double-helix ribbon model' rotates beside a twist dial; do not draw the ribbon or molecule. The lens then visits 'occupied space'. A plain opaque silhouette labelled 'space occupied, schematic' expands to fill a bounding box; do not draw atoms or circles. Both cards shrink beside the letter strip. Orange masks cover their unreadable base-order areas.

scenes.tts: Now predict. You need to show which bases face each other across the strands. Which model should move under the question lens? Hold your answer.
scenes.caption: Now predict. You need to show which bases face each other across the strands. Which model should move under the question lens? Hold your answer.
scenes.narration: Now predict. You need to show which bases face each other across the strands. Which model should move under the question lens? Hold your answer.
scenes.visual: Arrange the labelled-block ladder, shape card, letter strip and occupied-area silhouette evenly around the DNA sample. The yellow lens waits at center above the large question 'Which bases face each other?' All candidates continue a faint ambient drift. No molecular structure is drawn.
Deliberate predict pause. The question remains. The yellow lens breathes slowly while each candidate model drifts by a few pixels. No answer is highlighted.

scenes.tts: The ladder moves forward because its rungs expose pairing. The other models slide back, still useful for other questions. Choose D N A models by the question; every model leaves features out.
scenes.caption: The ladder moves forward because its rungs expose pairing. The other models slide back, still useful for other questions. Choose DNA models by the question; every model leaves features out.
scenes.narration: The ladder moves forward because its rungs expose pairing. The other models slide back, still useful for other questions. Choose DNA models by the question; every model leaves features out.
scenes.visual: The ladder glides under the yellow lens and fills most of the frame. Its paired blocks pulse GREEN. The shape card, letter strip and occupied-area silhouette remain visible but smaller, each beside its own short question label. The guiding rule appears briefly along the bottom, then fades while the world stays in place.

scenes.tts: Usefulness is not enough. Evidence can reject a model. Measured base amounts were close in pairs: adenine with thymine, and guanine with cytosine. A structure model had to explain that pattern, or be ruled out.
scenes.caption: Usefulness is not enough. Evidence can reject a model. Measured base amounts were close in pairs: adenine with thymine, and guanine with cytosine. A structure model had to explain that pattern, or be ruled out.
scenes.narration: Usefulness is not enough. Evidence can reject a model. Measured base amounts were close in pairs: adenine with thymine, and guanine with cytosine. A structure model had to explain that pattern, or be ruled out.
scenes.visual: PURPLE evidence cards slide from the toolbox into a filter track labelled 'structure models'. The first card reads 'base amounts'. Two balance bars appear, labelled A–T and G–C, with equal heights within each pair. No numerical values are invented. Only candidate structure arrangements that claim how bases pair pass through the filter; a candidate whose predicted pairing conflicts with A close to T and G close to C turns ORANGE and moves aside. The letter strip and the other task-specific views wait outside the track under a GREY label 'answers a different question'; they are not rejected.

scenes.tts: X ray diffraction added distances, width, and shape clues. It came from spots made by lined-up fibers. The pattern was indirect evidence, not a photograph of bases.
scenes.caption: X-ray diffraction added distances, width, and shape clues. It came from spots made by lined-up fibers. The pattern was indirect evidence, not a photograph of bases.
scenes.narration: X-ray diffraction added distances, width, and shape clues. It came from spots made by lined-up fibers. The pattern was indirect evidence, not a photograph of bases.
scenes.visual: The next PURPLE card reads 'X-ray diffraction'. A beam crosses a bundle labelled 'lined-up DNA fibers' and reaches a detector. A simplified spot pattern appears with a permanent label 'schematic, not a photograph'. Measurement arrows extend between spots, then transfer as constraint bars onto the surviving model card.

scenes.tts: Chemistry supplied another filter. Watson and Crick built a model fitting all the constraints. Backbones stayed outside, bases paired inside, and the strands ran in opposite directions.
scenes.caption: Chemistry supplied another filter. Watson and Crick built a model fitting all the constraints. Backbones stayed outside, bases paired inside, and the strands ran in opposite directions.
scenes.narration: Chemistry supplied another filter. Watson and Crick built a model fitting all the constraints. Backbones stayed outside, bases paired inside, and the strands ran in opposite directions.
scenes.visual: A PURPLE card labelled 'chemistry' joins the track. Plain GREY outside rails and BLUE paired blocks assemble into a wide schematic model, filling the frame. Opposite arrowheads travel along the rails to show direction. The surviving constraint cards snap around it like a testing frame. No molecular structure or atoms appear.

scenes.tts: Pairing also suggested a copying idea. Separate the strands, and each row fixes the matching row beside it. That was a prediction the model made, not proof by itself.
scenes.caption: Pairing also suggested a copying idea. Separate the strands, and each row fixes the matching row beside it. That was a prediction the model made, not proof by itself.
scenes.narration: Pairing also suggested a copying idea. Separate the strands, and each row fixes the matching row beside it. That was a prediction the model made, not proof by itself.
scenes.visual: Keep the tested schematic model large. Its GREY rails slide apart without showing molecular detail. Loose BLUE labelled blocks move toward each exposed row and form matching partners. A PURPLE tag reading 'copying prediction' follows the motion, while a small ORANGE tag reads 'still to test'.

scenes.tts: The result was the double helix model. Watson and Crick still called it unproved. Franklin and Gosling called a helix highly probable. Later tests supported its main features.
scenes.caption: The result was the double helix model. Watson and Crick still called it unproved. Franklin and Gosling called a helix highly probable. Later tests supported its main features.
scenes.narration: The result was the double helix model. Watson and Crick still called it unproved. Franklin and Gosling called a helix highly probable. Later tests supported its main features.
scenes.visual: Keep the labelled-block model flat and place a large rotating twist dial beside it; do not bend it into a molecular structure. Two cautious PURPLE tags appear, each with its authors: 'Watson and Crick: unproved' and 'Franklin and Gosling: highly probable (a helix)'. A timeline with dates shown only on screen extends rightward. Later test cards arrive and stamp GREEN checks onto the model's main features.

scenes.tts: Return to the original sample. Pairing, shape, order, and occupied space still need different views. Start with the question, then inspect what your chosen view hides.
scenes.caption: Return to the original sample. Pairing, shape, order, and occupied space still need different views. Start with the question, then inspect what your chosen view hides.
scenes.narration: Return to the original sample. Pairing, shape, order, and occupied space still need different views. Start with the question, then inspect what your chosen view hides.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the opening DNA sample box. The four question frames settle around it. The labelled-block ladder, shape card, letter strip and occupied-area silhouette enter their frames, each with an ORANGE 'leaves out' tab. The yellow lens makes one final circuit and stops on 'order', handing off to the second film.
End card shows one line only: 'Choose DNA models by the question; every model leaves features out.' The dimmed question frames drift behind it, with the yellow lens moving slowly.
